questions.stem: The barcode scanner won't read a client's wristband before a scheduled medication. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Scan a spare wristband taped to the bedside table
Get a new wristband printed, apply it, and then scan
Give the medication without scanning because the nurse knows the client
Skip the dose and document the scanner problem

rationale.correct: Barcode workarounds cause errors; correct the problem and complete the check.

perOption.a: Scanning anything other than the band on the client defeats the safety check.
perOption.b: Fix the problem rather than working around the system.
perOption.d: Missing a dose isn't necessary; fix the wristband.

questions.stem: Which abbreviations or notations should the nurse avoid because they are on the Joint Commission "Do Not Use" list? Select all that apply.

options.text: "U" for units
"QD" for daily
A trailing zero, as in 5.0 mg
A leading zero, as in 0.5 mg
"MS" for morphine sulfate
"mL" for milliliters

rationale.correct: Write "units", "daily", use leading zeros and never trailing zeros, and write out drug names.

perOption.a: Can be misread as 0 or 4, causing large insulin errors.
perOption.b: Can be confused with QID.
perOption.c: The decimal can be missed, causing a 10-fold overdose.
perOption.d: Leading zeros are required before a decimal point.
perOption.e: Can be confused with magnesium sulfate.

questions.stem: The nurse is programming an IV pump for a heparin infusion. The pump's drug library warns that the rate exceeds the hard limit. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Override the limit and start the infusion
Stop and recheck the order, concentration and calculation
Program the infusion as a basic infusion outside the drug library
Ask another nurse to start the infusion

rationale.correct: Smart pump alerts are a safety net; investigate them rather than bypass them.

perOption.a: Hard limits can't be overridden because the dose is likely dangerous.
perOption.b: The alert often means a programming or calculation error.
perOption.c: Bypassing the library removes the safety check.

questions.stem: The pharmacy stocks hydroxyzine and hydralazine in the same bin. Which strategy best reduces the risk of a mix-up?

options.text: Store look-alike, sound-alike drugs separately and use tall-man lettering
Ask nurses to read labels more carefully
Remove both drugs from the unit
Label the bin "Use caution"

rationale.correct: System fixes (separation, tall-man lettering, barcoding) work better than warnings.

perOption.a: Separation and tall-man lettering (hydrOXYzine, hydrALAZINE) reduce confusion.
perOption.b: Relying only on vigilance isn't a system fix.

questions.stem: For each situation, indicate whether the nurse should proceed or stop and clarify.

rows.text: An order reads "metoprolol 25 mg PO BID" and the client's heart rate is 78/min
An order reads "insulin regular 10 U subcut"
An order reads "morphine 2 mg IV every 2 hours as needed" without an indication
An order reads "furosemide 40 mg IV daily" and the potassium is 4.2 mEq/L

rationale.correct: Clarify incomplete or error-prone orders before giving medication.

perOption.r1:c1: The order is complete and the parameter is safe.
perOption.r2:c2: Clarify and have the order written with "units".
perOption.r3:c2: Clarify the indication (for example, pain rated 4 to 6).
perOption.r4:c1: Order and potassium level are acceptable.

questions.stem: An infant security alarm sounds on the postpartum unit. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Check that all infants are with their mothers or in the nursery and watch exits per the facility's code
Turn off the alarm
Leave the unit to look for the infant in the parking lot
Wait for security to arrive before doing anything

perOption.a: The infant abduction code calls for securing exits and accounting for every infant.
perOption.b: The alarm must be investigated.
perOption.c: Follow the code; security handles the search.

questions.stem: Which actions are part of a surgical site infection (SSI) prevention bundle? Select all that apply.

options.text: Giving the prophylactic antibiotic within 60 minutes before the incision
Removing hair with clippers rather than a razor, if hair removal is needed
Keeping glucose controlled around surgery
Keeping the client warm during surgery
Shaving the site the night before surgery
Continuing prophylactic antibiotics for 7 days after routine surgery

rationale.correct: SSI prevention: timely antibiotics, clippers, glucose control, normothermia.

perOption.a: Gives effective tissue levels at the time of incision.
perOption.b: Razors cause small cuts that raise infection risk.
perOption.d: Normothermia supports immune function and healing.

questions.stem: For each intervention, indicate the healthcare-associated infection or infections it helps prevent. Each row may have more than one answer.

Daily review of whether the device is still needed

Keep the drainage bag below the bladder

perOption.r2:c1: Remove catheters as soon as possible.
perOption.r2:c2: Remove central lines as soon as possible.
perOption.r2:c3: Daily sedation breaks and weaning checks shorten ventilation.

questions.stem: How should the nurse clean a shared blood pressure cuff between clients on a medical unit?

options.text: Wipe it with an approved disinfectant and allow the contact time on the label
Rinse it with tap water
Leave it uncleaned if it looks clean
Sterilize it in an autoclave after each use

perOption.a: Low-level disinfection with proper contact time kills common organisms.
perOption.b: Water doesn't disinfect.
perOption.c: Organisms can be present without visible soil.
perOption.d: Non-critical items need disinfection, not sterilization.

questions.stem: Before defibrillating a client, what should the nurse do?

options.text: Make sure no one is touching the client or bed and say "All clear"
Leave oxygen flowing across the chest
Apply pads over a medication patch
Wet the client's chest

rationale.correct: Defibrillation safety: clear everyone, remove oxygen and patches from the field, dry chest.

perOption.a: Prevents electric shock to staff.
perOption.b: Oxygen near the paddles can cause fire; move it away.
perOption.c: Remove patches; they can cause burns.
perOption.d: Water can conduct current and cause burns.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing a new graduate's medication administration. Highlight the actions that are unsafe.

segments.text: identified the client using name and date of birth
prepared medications for two clients at the same time
crushed an extended-release tablet to mix with applesauce
